topic: Fundamentals of Linear Algebra: Understanding Vectors

outline.topic: Fundamentals of Linear Algebra: Understanding Vectors

sections.title: Introduction: What is a Vector?
sections.content: Define vectors as both geometric arrows (direction and magnitude) and ordered lists of numbers (coordinates). Explain the transition from 1D scalar lines to 2D/3D space.
sections.example: Visualize a robotic arm: The vector describes the position of the claw tip relative to the base (x, y coordinates).

sections.title: Vector Addition: The Head-to-Tail Rule
sections.content: Introduce vector addition geometrically. Explain that adding two vectors v and w results in a new vector by placing the tail of w at the head of v.
sections.example: A bird flying: Vector 1 is the bird's velocity; Vector 2 is the wind velocity. Their sum shows the bird's actual resultant path across the ground.

sections.title: Scalar Multiplication: Stretching Space
sections.content: Explain multiplying a vector by a scalar. Discuss how it changes magnitude (scaling) and direction (flipping if negative) while maintaining the original slope.
sections.example: A magnifying glass effect: Multiplying a character's position vector by 2.0 scales their distance from the origin while keeping the angle constant.

sections.title: Linear Combinations and Basis Vectors
sections.content: Introduce the unit basis vectors i-hat (1,0) and j-hat (0,1). Explain that any vector in 2D space can be represented as a scaled combination of these two basis vectors.
sections.example: A character in a grid-based video game moving 3 units Right (i) and 2 units Up (j) to reach coordinates (3, 2).

sections.title: Conclusion and Application Summary
sections.content: Briefly recap how linear algebra acts as the 'language of motion' in computer graphics, data science, and physics simulations.
sections.example: Explain how a 3D model in a game is just a collection of thousands of vectors being transformed by these math rules in real-time.

storyboard.title: Introduction: What is a Vector?
lecture_lines: Vectors are arrows representing direction and magnitude.
They can also be lists of numbers.
Think of them as positions in space.
animations: Create a 2D arrow at the origin labeled 'Vector v' in color #FF0000.
Animate the arrow sliding to a new position.
Change the arrow's color to #00FF00 to show displacement.
Add a label 'v = (x, y)' near the vector.
Pulse the arrow to emphasize it represents a movement.

storyboard.title: Vector Addition: The Head-to-Tail Rule
lecture_lines: Vector addition uses the head-to-tail rule.
Place the second tail at the first head.
The result is a new, single vector.
animations: Show two vectors 'u' and 'v' starting at origin.
Move the tail of vector 'v' to the head of 'u'.
Draw a resultant vector 'u+v' from origin to 'v''s head.

storyboard.title: Scalar Multiplication: Stretching Space
lecture_lines: Scalars stretch or shrink a vector's length.
A negative scalar flips the direction.
The line's slope remains constant throughout.
animations: Scale 'v' by factor 2 to double its length.
Scale 'v' by factor -1 to flip its direction.

storyboard.title: Linear Combinations and Basis Vectors
lecture_lines: Basis vectors i-hat and j-hat span the space.
Every vector is a scaled combination of these.
Grid coordinates map directly to these scales.
animations: Show a vector 'v' as a combination of 'i' and 'j'.
Highlight the grid formed by 'i' and 'j'.

storyboard.title: Conclusion and Application Summary
lecture_lines: Linear algebra is the language of motion.
It powers computer graphics and physics.
Models are just collections of many vectors.
animations: Fade in all vectors discussed: 'u', 'v', and 'u+v'.
Highlight the combined space formed by all linear combinations.
Show a 'Summary' text box with key takeaways.
